6.1 Final Model¶

Fitting the Pipeline of 5.6 on the 1440 Videos¶

The pipeline delivered in 5.6, StandardScaler → SVC(C = 1), with probability=True so that it returns the probability of each emotion.

In [5]:
final_model = Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()),
                        ("svc", SVC(kernel="rbf", C=cfg.C_FIXED, probability=True, random_state=cfg.SEED))])
final_model.fit(full_table, y_full);

Saving the Model¶

Out[6]:
['/Users/andreleao/Documents/MIA/1ANO/IAC/Emotion_Recognition/app/model.joblib']

Answer 6.1¶

The pipeline chosen in 5.6 is fitted on all 1440 videos of the 24 actors and saved to app/model.joblib.

In classifier.py, load_model reads model.joblib, and predict receives the frames of the clip in pixels, normalises them with normalise_d, computes the 55 features with video_features, and returns the probability of each emotion from predict_proba. Both functions are imported from our src modules, the same used for training, placed inside the app folder.

An SVC returns probabilities only with probability=True: it then fits a sigmoid on its decision values with an internal cross-validation (Platt scaling).

6.2 Predictions on Our Own Clips¶

Each member recorded one clip per emotion in the application, saying "Kids are talking by the door". The landmarks of each clip were downloaded from the page and saved in recordings/ as <member>_<emotion>.csv. The probabilities are recomputed here with the same two calls as predict in classifier.py.

Predictions on Our Own Clips and Results Table¶

In [7]:
REC_PATH = cfg.ROOT / "recordings"
EMOTION_NAMES = [cfg.EMOTIONS[code] for code in final_model.classes_]

rec_frames, rec_features, rec_proba = {}, {}, {}
for file in sorted(REC_PATH.glob("*.csv")):           # one file per clip: <member>_<emotion>.csv
    member, emotion = file.stem.split("_")
    frames = pd.read_csv(file)                        # the CSV downloaded from the app, in pixels
    features = ftrs.video_features(norm.normalise_d(frames))   # the same two calls as predict()

    rec_frames[(member, emotion)] = frames
    rec_features[(member, emotion)] = features
    rec_proba[(member, emotion)] = final_model.predict_proba(features.to_frame().T)[0]

proba = pd.DataFrame(rec_proba, index=EMOTION_NAMES).T
proba.index.names = ["member", "emotion"]

predictions = pd.DataFrame({"n_frames": [len(f) for f in rec_frames.values()],
                            "predicted": proba.idxmax(axis=1),
                            "p_predicted": proba.max(axis=1)}, index=proba.index)
predictions["p_true"] = [proba.loc[i, i[1]] for i in proba.index]
predictions["rank_true"] = [int((proba.loc[i] > proba.loc[i, i[1]]).sum()) + 1 for i in proba.index]
predictions["correct"] = predictions["predicted"] == predictions.index.get_level_values("emotion")

print("Correct:", predictions["correct"].sum(), "of", len(predictions))
predictions.round(3)

Answer 6.2¶

7 of the 16 clips are classified correctly (44 %), against 12.5 % by chance. The probabilities recomputed from the downloaded CSVs are the ones shown by the page (64.4 % angry and 26.4 % surprised for André's surprised clip in the screenshot above, 35.1 % surprised for Miguel's surprised clip).

Recognised:

  • Disgust (2 of 2), with the highest confidences of all clips (0.98 and 0.75). It is a strong, unusual expression, and our feature M10 (upper lip towards the nose) targets it.
  • Sad (2 of 2), but this says little: sad is predicted for 7 of the 16 clips.
  • Angry, surprised and happy in one of the two clips each. For angry and surprised the true emotion was second where it failed. André's happy clip was not close: sad 0.39, happy 0.03.

Not recognised:

  • Neutral (0 of 2) and calm (0 of 2): predicted as sad or neutral. These are the low-movement expressions that already overlapped under LOSO (4.4), where sad was the default class for quiet faces. André's neutral clip was close: sad 0.49, neutral 0.43.
  • Fearful (0 of 2): predicted as sad and surprised, the confusion of fear with surprise already seen in 4.4.

The pattern is the one of the LOSO confusion matrix (4.4), only stronger. Strong, distinctive expressions are recognised, subtle ones and fear are not. Sixteen clips from two people are too few for a score, but the result is below the LOSO estimate (macro F1 0.557).

6.3 Our Clips in the Training Distribution¶

Each feature of each clip is located in its distribution over the 1440 training videos, as a percentile (0 = below every training video, 100 = above every one). A feature is outside the range when it is below the minimum or above the maximum of the training videos.

In [11]:
rec_table = pd.DataFrame(rec_features).T[full_table.columns]
rec_table.index.names = ["member", "emotion"]

percentiles = rec_table.apply(lambda col: col.apply(lambda v: percentileofscore(full_table[col.name], v)))
below = rec_table < full_table.min()
above = rec_table > full_table.max()
outside = below | above

Comparison Table of the two Normalisations¶

In [16]:
def mouth_width(frames):
    return ftrs.euclidean_distance(frames, 48, 54).median()

def iod_pixels(frames):
    return ftrs.euclidean_distance(frames, 36, 45).median()

neutral = full_df[full_df["emotion"] == 1]
rows = {}
for name, normalise in [("by d", norm.normalise_d), ("by 1280 x 720", norm.normalise_image)]:
    actors = neutral.groupby("actor").apply(lambda g: mouth_width(normalise(g)))
    rows[name] = {"actors_min": actors.min(), "actors_max": actors.max(),
                  "andre": mouth_width(normalise(rec_frames[("andre", "neutral")])),
                  "miguel": mouth_width(normalise(rec_frames[("miguel", "neutral")]))}
iod = neutral.groupby("actor").apply(iod_pixels)
rows["d in pixels"] = {"actors_min": iod.min(), "actors_max": iod.max(),
                       "andre": iod_pixels(rec_frames[("andre", "neutral")]),
                       "miguel": iod_pixels(rec_frames[("miguel", "neutral")])}

Answer 6.3¶

Most features fall inside the training range, but not in its centre. Of the 16 × 55 values, 46 fall outside the range, all but one below the minimum. The median percentile by statistic is 43 for the mean, 31 for the std, 24 for the range, 20 for the energy and 16 for the velocity. The position of the face is roughly typical, but its movement is systematically lower than in the training videos.

Which features fall outside, and why:

  • The brow shape, own_M11 (velocity below the minimum in 11 clips, energy in 10). The mean of M11 is also at the 0–15th percentile in every clip, of both members and every emotion. A shift that is the same for every person and every emotion is not an expression: it comes from the tracker. The 68 points are mapped from the MediaPipe mesh, whose brow points are not placed exactly as OpenFace places them, so the brows come out flatter and steadier. The same applies, less strongly, to the mean mouth width (M2_mean, median percentile 5).
  • The velocity and energy of other measures (own_M9, M2, own_M10, M6, M4): motion lower than in any training video. Possible causes, which these clips cannot separate:
    • the tracker: MediaPipe in video mode follows the face from frame to frame and jitters less than OpenFace, whose jitter adds a floor of motion to every training video;
    • the camera: Miguel's camera delivered about 20 frames per second (screenshot of 6.2), which the app interpolated to 30. Linear interpolation smooths the trajectories, lowering velocity and especially energy;
    • the person: we are not professional actors and moved less.
  • The range is low (24th percentile) partly because our clips are shorter. Miguel's have 68–97 frames, below the training minimum of 88 in most cases. A shorter clip gives the face less time to reach its extremes. Miguel's ranges are lower than André's (16th vs 32nd percentile), whose clips have about 108 frames, the training median.
  • André's neutral clip has 18 features below the minimum. He kept his face almost still, while every training video shows an actor speaking.
  • The only value above the maximum is M5_vel in Miguel's fearful clip. Miguel's eye-opening statistics (M5) are high in every clip (above the 90th percentile), probably blinks, which MediaPipe follows closely.

These shifts explain part of 6.2. Lower motion makes the clips look like the quiet training classes, which is why sad and neutral are predicted for 8 of the 16 clips.

The normalisation by 1280 × 720 would have failed. On the neutral clips, the median mouth width normalised by d is 0.525 (André) and 0.567 (Miguel), against 0.551–0.664 for the 24 actors: close to, or inside, the training range. Normalised by 1280 × 720, André's is 0.143, against 0.082–0.111: 29 % above the largest actor. Dividing by the image size assumes the face has the same size in pixels as in the dataset. That depends on the camera's resolution and on the distance to it: André's inter-ocular distance is 349 pixels, against 187–228 for the actors. Miguel's value falls inside the range only by coincidence, because his face (235 pixels) happened to be about the size of the actors'. The normalisation by d measures the face with the face itself, so it doesn't depend on the camera, the resolution or the distance.

6.4 Frame Rate¶

If a camera records at 15 frames per second and the clip reaches predict without resampling, each pair of consecutive frames is 1/15 s apart instead of 1/30 s. We simulate it by keeping every other frame of our 30-fps clips, and compare the features and the predictions.

In [17]:
ratios, preds_15 = {}, {}
for key, frames in rec_frames.items():
    frames_15 = frames.iloc[::2]                                   # every other frame: 15 fps, not resampled
    features_15 = ftrs.video_features(norm.normalise_d(frames_15))
    ratios[key] = features_15 / rec_features[key]
    preds_15[key] = EMOTION_NAMES[final_model.predict_proba(features_15.to_frame().T)[0].argmax()]

ratios = pd.DataFrame(ratios).T
display(ratios.T.groupby(statistic).median().T.describe().loc[["min", "50%", "max"]].round(2))

at_15 = pd.DataFrame({"predicted_30fps": predictions["predicted"], "predicted_15fps": pd.Series(preds_15)})
print("Correct at 30 fps:", predictions["correct"].sum(),
      "| at 15 fps:", (at_15["predicted_15fps"] == at_15.index.get_level_values(1)).sum())

Answer 6.4¶

The statistics of position do not change, those of movement do.

  • Mean, std and range describe the values of the measure, not the time between them. Keeping every other frame keeps the same face at half as many moments, so they barely change (ratios 0.96 to 1.01 in our clips). The range can only shrink slightly, if an extreme fell on a dropped frame.
  • Velocity and energy increase. Both are per frame. At 15 fps a frame lasts twice as long, so for a smooth movement each difference covers twice the change: v roughly doubles and E roughly quadruples. In our clips v rises by 1.80–1.95 and E by 3.0–3.6. Both are slightly below 2 and 4 because part of each difference is tracker jitter, which is not larger over a longer interval.

The model would then see faces that move twice as fast. It learnt what fast and slow mean from videos at 30 fps, so the same expression would look much more active. In our clips, 12 of the 16 predictions at 15 fps become angry, the emotion with the most movement, and the correct predictions drop from 7 to 5. Only 3 clips that were wrong at 30 fps become right, which reads as chance, not as an improvement.

The frame rate is part of the definition of the features. Velocity and energy are measured per frame, not per second, so the model only means anything when the frame rate matches the 30 fps of the training data. That's why the app resamples every clip to 30 fps before predict. Alternatively, the features could be expressed per second, which removes the dependence on the frame rate of the camera, as long as training and application use the same convention.

Answer 7.1¶

Changed the result most:¶

  • Evaluation protocol: macro F1 0.752 with the random split vs 0.557 under LOSO (4.3). The random split lets the model recognise faces it has already seen.
  • Reducing the features: ANOVA K = 5 loses 0.21 (5.3) and PCA 75 % loses 0.095 (5.2). The information is spread over many weak features, so all 55 are kept.
  • C, but only below 1. The score goes from 0.388 at C = 0.01 to 0.557 at C = 1 (4.5).

Did not change it:¶

  • Own features (+0.032), PCA 95 % (−0.019), C ≥ 1 (≤ 0.024): all within the standard error of a LOSO mean (≈ 0.033).
  • Nesting the choice of C. The nested score (0.5575) equals the best point of the curve (0.5574), because C = 1 won 19 of the 20 folds (4.6). The optimism of 4.5 was small in practice, but nesting is still the only honest estimate.
  • The treatment of outliers. The flagged frames were kept (2.3).
  • Normalisation, inside the dataset: actors sit at similar distances from the camera (2.1). It only mattered in the app, where face size in pixels varies (6.3).

The largest source of variation was not a decision but the person: the score of a single actor ranges from 0.325 to 0.923 (4.2), more than any decision moved the mean.

Answer 7.2¶

LOSO and the test both measure performance on a new actor recorded with the RAVDESS protocol, not on a real user. Our own clips confirm the gap: 7 of 16 correct (44 %), against an accuracy of about 0.58.

  • Professional actors: clear, exaggerated expressions, half at strong intensity. Real users move less (6.3: movement features at the 16th–20th percentile). With only 24 similar actors, the score on different people is unknown.
  • Emotions on request: the label is the portrayed emotion, not a felt one. Real expressions are spontaneous, subtle and mixed, the face is mostly neutral.
  • Two statements: every video is one of two spoken sentences, so the mouth features mostly describe speech (4.4, 5.5). Silence or other sentences fall outside the training data, and clip length is set by the protocol (1.4).
  • One frontal camera: same view, lighting, frame rate and tracker. The normalisation does not correct head rotation (actor 15, 2.3), and the app's tracker and cameras shift the features (6.3, 6.4).

What the scores do say. LOSO and the test measure how well the model generalises to a new person, but not to a new situation: a different way of expressing emotion, different speech, a different camera. For the users of a real application they are an upper bound. To estimate that performance, the test set would have to be recorded in the application's conditions, with spontaneous expressions, varied people and ordinary cameras.
